lines.note: Honshi is the original teacher; honno shishō makes that relation explicit. Primeiro and proprio continue into mestre on the following row. No final full stop is visible after proprio.

runs.text: meſtre. i, Xaca. Como cuidão os gentios.

lines.note: The gloss identifies the teacher as Xaca, Shaka, and qualifies this as the belief of the gentios. Xaca is italic here, embedded in the Portuguese sentence rather than a new headword.
Honshin, one's original mind, is referred to the preferred form honjin with Meliùs. This is the dictionary's own pronunciation preference, not grounds to change the first headword.
Sentido and juizo describe the proper senses or judgment. Fonxinni begins the locative phrase completed by motozzuqu on the next row.

runs.text: Tornar em ſeu acordo, ou juizo.

lines.note: Honshin ni motozuku is explained as returning to one's senses or judgment. The zzu spelling represents the voiced dental series; it is not an accidental doubled z.
Honshiki denotes simplicity or candour in this gloss, not necessarily the modern dominant sense of formal or authentic style. Candura is retained as printed.
The adjectival honshiki-na is glossed as simple and candid. The final Fon- belongs to the following alternative, not to the Portuguese definition.
This completes Fon-xiqiùdo, approximately honshikyūdo, a person of that character; Idem repeats the preceding sense. The visible u mark is retained rather than supplied from morphology.
Honshō is one's true judgment or consciousness. The second occurrence takes object marker uo and leads into losing consciousness.
Ushinō, lose, completes honshō o ushinō. Portuguese gives both loss of reason and fainting; the printed open-o mark is maintained.
Honshō ni naru is explained as coming to oneself again. A clear initial pilcrow introduces this example; Item then opens a further Buddhist sense.

runs.text: Suſtancia como eſpiritu de que ſe falla no

lines.note: The additional sense is a substance likened to spirit in Buddhist teaching. The scan reads Suſtancia, not the garbled OCR buſtanũa; the internal consonant group is visible.
Buppô completes the reference to Buddhist doctrine. The word is italic in this location; its circumflex is visible and is not a grave accent.
Honshoku is an original office or dignity. Offiçio retains the printed cedilla, independently of modern Portuguese spelling.
Honshu denotes the proper or true lord. The Portuguese establishes ownership or lordship, not the geographical name Honshū.

runs.text: Explicar algũa couſa por outra lin

lines.note: Honyaku is explaining something in another language. The last lin continues lingua below; no division sign is inferred from that continuation alone.

runs.text: gua, ou traduzir em outra lingua. Vt,

lines.note: The alternative Portuguese explanation is translating into another language. Vt introduces the example split Fon-/yacu across the rows.
Yacu ſuru completes honyaku suru, to translate. This short physical row is part of the example, not a separate lexical entry.
Honza is referred to honza no shu. The following full entry explains the established or long-serving members of a household.

runs.text: Serra, ou monte principal onde vão

lines.note: Honzan is the principal mountain or religious centre. The pilgrimage clause continues below; the gloss should not be reduced to a purely topographical mountain.
Em romaria supplies the religious sense: the gentios go there on pilgrimage. This completes the preceding relative clause.
Honza no shu and honzashu name established household people or servants. The Portuguese cria- continues criados, not a new word on the next row.

runs.text: dos antigos que ha muito tempo ſeruem a al-

lines.note: These are old servants who have served a lord for a long time. Tempo is supported by both the visible p and the temporal construction, correcting temoo.
After completing algum senhor, the contrasting shinzashu introduces newer servants. Its shin- contrasts with the preceding established honza group.

runs.text: tempo começarão a ſeruir a algum ſenhor.

lines.note: The new servants began serving only recently. The temporal ha pouco tempo contrasts explicitly with ha muito tempo in the earlier definition.
Honzon is the principal object of worship. Idolo and pagode are the missionaries' Portuguese terms for the image, not a claim that the Japanese word means a building here.

The phrase Foppôuôno ſanjin concerns the three bodies or aspects of the Buddhist principle. The initial headword's marks are worn; the fuller repeated example supplies comparison, but its clearer marks do not justify inventing missing strokes.

runs.text: maneiras de attributos, ou qualidades que ha

lines.note: Tres maneiras de attributos describes three kinds of attributes or qualities. Enlarged type supports attributos, replacing the nonword atricutos.

runs.text: naquelle primeiro principio de que ſe fala no

lines.note: The attributes belong to that first principle discussed in Buddhist teaching. Primeiro principio is the Portuguese conceptual framing, not an additional Japanese expression.
Buppô completes the Buddhist reference. The whole word is italic, including B, and the mark is a circumflex rather than the OCR grave.

runs.text: Vapor, ou bafo que ſae da agua quen-

lines.note: Hoke is vapour rising from hot water. Bafo means breath or steam; the f is visible and semantically fits, unlike baſo.
Hoke ga tatsu means the vapour rises. The definition repeats this in Portuguese with Aleuantarſe, while quen-/te completes the description of hot water.
The vapour is again called bafo. The letters belong to one word; the OCR's internal space split the a from the f without a comparable word gap.
Hōqe, quru, eta gives the inflections of becoming foolish or losing one's wits. The printed long vowel and the older verbal form are retained rather than modernized to bokeru.
Hōqeta fito and hōqemono both describe a foolish person. The Portuguese Par continues paruo below; a missing end mark is not supplied on morphological grounds.
Uo completes paruo, followed by synonymous tolo. This is a short continuation of the previous definition, not independent page furniture.
Hōkei is an honorific kindness or favour, glossed kōbashii megumi. Enlargement shows the caron in Cǒbaxij, omitted by OCR; megumi and Beneficios support the benefaction sense.

runs.text: mos, & afabilidade que ſe mostra a alguem

lines.note: Mimos and afabilidade explain favours and affability shown to someone. The visible ascender in the latter supports d rather than OCR c.
Falando com corteſia specifies courteous speech; S marks written usage. It qualifies the preceding honorific expression, not the following sword entry.
Hōken, takara no ken, is a precious sword. Tenxǒdai- begins Tenshō Daijin, named as the sword's owner; the Japanese name is upright within the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: que he hua das tres peças prezadas que tẽ

lines.note: The enlarged first types read jin, completing Tenxǒdai-jin, not ju. The sword is described as one of three treasured objects, connecting the explanation to the imperial regalia.
Dairi names the imperial holder of the treasures. Item adds the king's sword as a further sense, then introduces the synonym on the next row.
Guioqen is gyoken, the imperial sword. It belongs to the preceding i, explanation and is not a fresh alphabetically placed heading.
Hoket-, chi o oginō, means replenishing the blood. The checked final t is not an omitted vowel, and Portuguese temperar or refazer supplies the medical sense.
Fazer completes refazer o sangue, to restore the blood. The final S is the written-usage label.
Hōket and Dairi denote the imperial palace. Its marked vowel distinguishes this entry from the immediately preceding blood-replenishing word.
Hoki denotes a high place such as a precipice. Alto and precipicio are recoverable in the scan, unlike OCR lto and preipotio. The final Foqi begins the cross-column example.
Hoki kara votçuru means falling from that height. Enlargement supports the round o in votçuru, a historical form related to falling; it is not the garbled vntçuru.
Perigoſo completes the description of the high, dangerous place. The row belongs to the cross-column falling example.
Hoki, ki o oginō, replenishes vital energy. Taking medicine supplies the practical explanation; this is distinct from the preceding geographical hoki.

runs.text: ra o coração, ou pera refazer os eſpiritus vi-

lines.note: The medicines are for the heart or restoration of the vital spirits. Vi- continues vitaes, the historical Portuguese physiological terminology.
Taes completes vitaes. S marks the Japanese expression as written usage, rather than being part of the Latin-derived medical phrase.
Hōqi, nori no hata, is a banner of the doctrine or sect. Fata is the Japanese word hata, not a Portuguese noun.
The sect's banner is raised: hōqi o aguru. Portuguese aleuantar explains the action; bã- continues bandeira, not an independent abbreviation.

runs.text: deira dalgũa ſeita, ou lei diuulgandoa.

lines.note: Deira completes bandeira: propagating a sect or law is likened to raising its flag. The scan has deira, not OCR detira; no extra t is present.

Hōki means an armed uprising, so the paraphrase is linguistically expected to be tachi okoru. Enlargement nevertheless shows Fachi, with an F-like middle arm; retain the printed reading and flag a possible printing error rather than silently supplying Tachi.
Zantō shosho ni hōki su describes the remnants rising in various places. The Portuguese gloss specifies many people assembling under arms; fô- continues the verb on the next row.

runs.text: O restante da gente aleuantouſe com

lines.note: Qiſu completes hōki su. The remaining people rose up; the Portuguese rest- spelling is retained without treating its s shape as a linguistic correction.
The uprising takes place with warfare throughout the localities. Pellos is the printed historical contraction, not modern pelos.
Hōki, takara no utsuwamono, means precious vessels. The Japanese gloss distinguishes this homophone from an uprising or a religious banner.
Other rich objects are included alongside vessels. Peças refers to articles or objects here, not theatrical pieces.
Hōki is a broom. The caron distinguishes its historical vowel from nearby circumflex headwords; Portuguese vaſoura supplies an unambiguous gloss.
Hōkiboshi is a comet, literally the broom star. The dictionary prefers Qiacuxei, kyakusei, rather than rejecting the vernacular compound.

runs.text: Adu. Aquelle modo de ſoar a cou

lines.note: Hokihoki is an adverbial sound description. The account begins the noise of something breaking, with cou continuing couſa across the row boundary.

runs.text: ſa quando ſe quebra como pao ſeco, &c.

lines.note: Dry wood is the example of the cracking sound. Pao ſeco is historical Portuguese and should not be modernized to pão seco in Level 1.

runs.text: Certa erua de que ſe fazem vaſou-

lines.note: Hōkigusa is a plant used to make brooms. The compound's guſa corresponds to kusa with voicing, not a Portuguese word embedded in the definition.
In Cami the plant is called hōkigi. Por que introduces the reason for the tree-like name; the scan supports P rather than OCR F. Cami is italic here and remains so.

runs.text: he como plantaſinha de pois de grande.

lines.note: When grown, the plant resembles a small woody plant. De pois remains spaced as printed; it is not a reason to alter the botanical headword.
Hōkyō, takara no hako, is a treasure chest. The two accented vowels belong to separate moraic components, matching the Japanese box gloss.

runs.text: riquezas, ou õde estão metidas couſas precioſas.

lines.note: The chest holds wealth or precious things. Portuguese õde is an abbreviated onde, retained rather than expanded into the diplomatic text.
Hōkwa, hi o hanatsu, means setting fire. The definition begins a restriction on its customary uses; particu- continues particularly.

runs.text: lar mente ſe vſa quando queimão a caſa dalgum

lines.note: The term is especially used for burning a house. The visible separation in lar mente is retained even though the Portuguese word continues particularmente.

runs.text: malfeitor, ou quando poẽ fogo nas caſas, &

lines.note: Burning a wrongdoer's house and burning enemy houses are the specified cases. Malfeitor is the historical Portuguese noun, not a defective Japanese gloss.
Enemy settlements complete the second context. Iye o hōkwa introduces the Japanese example of setting fire to a house.
Suru completes the preceding Japanese phrase; Portuguese queimar a caſa translates the whole example. It is not an independent suru entry.

runs.text: Fogos que ſe fazem na China em ſinal

lines.note: This homophonous hōkwa is a Chinese beacon fire. Em ſinal means as a signal; the separate i and n are visible where OCR read ſmal.
The beacon signals an enemy incursion. Hōkwa o begins the example of raising the warning fire, distinct from the preceding arson sense.

runs.text: Aleuantar este fogo pera que a gen-

lines.note: Aguru completes raising the beacon. The scan supports Aleuantar, not Aleu intar; the object is the signal fire and gen- continues gente.

runs.text: te ſe ajunte, & ſe defenda dos inimigos q̃ vẽ.

lines.note: The people gather and defend themselves against approaching enemies. Defenda has meaningful f, not ſ; the scan and Portuguese grammar agree on the correction.

Hōkwan, takara no kamuri, is a rich crown. The second-pass enlargement clearly shows a caron, so the initial OCR reading is retained despite NINJAL's Fôquan. The external headword does not override the printed accent.
The crown is ornamented. S is the written-register label attached to this Japanese entry, not a fragment of the next headword.
Another hōkwan denotes a kind of flute. Historical frauta is retained and should not be normalized to flauta merely because that is modern Portuguese.
Hora means a cave or cavern. Dirt crosses ou, but the surviving strokes and the pairing cauerna/ou/lapa support ou rather than OCR ox.
Hōraku is a performance such as a play or dance. Auto is a theatrical piece in this context; the entry proceeds to its religious setting.

runs.text: ſe faz diante dos Camis, & Fotoques, ou por

lines.note: The performance is before Camis and Fotoques. Both borrowed Japanese religious terms appear italic in the scan; retain that typography and allow review toggling.

runs.text: reſpeito dalgum defunto ja de muito tempo.

lines.note: A performance may also commemorate someone long deceased. Defunto is supported by the scan and sense; OCR de ſunto split the word and confused f with ſ.
Hōraku suru means performing this entertainment. The complete Portuguese infinitival gloss makes the verbal use clear.
Horagai, also hora no kai, is a conch used to summon people. The worn intervening i is retained from the print; cha continues chamão on the next row without an invented hyphen.
Mão completes chamão, they call the people. The row is not the independent Portuguese noun mão, hand.
Hōran is glossed kōbashii araragi, a fragrant plant. The description identifies scent but does not justify assigning a modern botanical species from this line alone.
Ta completes certa: a particular fragrant herb. The continuation belongs to hōran, not to the following conch entry.

runs.text: Buzio com q̃ tangẽ como buzina.

lines.note: Hora no kai is the conch blown like a horn. Tangẽ is the printed nasal abbreviation of the verb, retained rather than expanded.
Hōrat, rachi o hanatsu, concerns unrestrained conduct. The worn initial F still has surviving strokes; restore it from OCR's ǒrat, supported by the headword sequence and NINJAL Fǒrat.

runs.text: deſcomedimento, ou pouca policia nas acçoẽs,

lines.note: The Portuguese gloss describes excess and lack of civility in actions. Policia here is civil order or comportment, not specifically a modern police force.
Catchword repeating the opening of f212. Its stable ID is retained, but it is not an additional body continuation; the continuous definition reaches &c. on the next page.
